content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a method to tackle a new online meta learning setting where the task boundaries are not known (no access or costly to obtain) or do not exist (e.g. gradual change). 

Meta learning consists of the meta-training step and the adaptation step. During the adaptation step, instead of re-setting the task parameter to the meta-parameter at the beginning of the task (e.g. requiring to know the task boundary to know when to reset), the proposed method uses regularisation to pull parameter back gradually and softly (see Fig. 1) thus does not require to know the task boundaries. 

Experiments show that the proposed method can learn new tasks faster than the state-of-the-art online learning methods on Rainbow-MNIST, CIFAR100 and CELEBA datasets.

content.title: Response to R4
content.comment:
We can add more examples and justification to the paper (we can't edit it at this time, but can revise the final). Here are a few examples that could be formalized with this problem setting:
- Users tagging things in their personal photo albums, where they might like to propagate labels to the entire photo album from a few annotations. In this case, each task might correspond to the particular concept the user wants to tag ("Hawaii vacation", "pictures of interesting birds", "cool car", etc.), and both the meaning of the concepts ("cool car" -- meaning changes over time as user preferences change) and their identity ("Hawaii vacation" might be a new concept introduced after user goes on vacation) might change over time.
- A home robot performing tasks based on user commands, where the user might want to teach the robot semantic concepts ("this is my favorite shirt, please have it cleaned") that might change over time (a different shirt might be the "favorite" next year), and where new concepts might be introduced ("this is my new jacket, take it to the closet"). The time at which the meaning of a concept changes (jacket is no longer "new") or a new concept is introduced is often not going to be explicitly indicated by the user.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes an extension of model adaptation via meta learning in an online fashion. This paper particularly targets the problem model adaptation in the environment with changing tasks and input distributions. With the ability for fast adaptation, the proposed method called as Fully-Online Meta-Learning (FOML) adapt the model parameters quickly and continuously for any incoming tasks. The experiments show that FOML can continuously adapt to a new task quickly and beat prior methods on meta-learning on several challenging datasets  e.g., Rainbow-MNIST, CIFAR100, and CELEBA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem of learning from constant stream of data with distinct tasks in this work is challenging and relevant to rapid online adaptation of neural networks for many real-world applications e.g., traffic predictions systems.
-  The formulation for online meta-learning is somewhat novel and uses no task boundary knowledge to learn from newly incoming tasks.
- The experiments show the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method to tackle online meta-learning problems compared to other prior arts e.g., FTML, LwF, iCARL, and MOCA.


Weaknesses:
- The definition and the role of task boundaries are not very clear for fully online meta learning and prior methods. Is this the boundary that has a task id indicating a specific task? What are “well-separated tasks”? How do the tasks for FOML have no boundaries? As understood from the FTML paper, Standard Online Meta Learning also does not need this additional knowledge to run the algorithm and adapt the model.  Does “task boundary” here mean that the evaluation task might come from past tasks i.e., not necessarily from the currently training tasks? Also, if there is no specified boundaries between tasks, can we derive the problem as standard online learning?
- The “gradual changes of tasks” also need to be explained in more detail. If there are no clear boundaries, how are tasks verified changed overtime? In my opinion, the motivation described in introduction does not perfectly align with the setting. It is vague to capture the gradual changes but discarding the concept of continual learning. The strong assumption in meta learning is about the stationarity of the data distribution. The gradual change of its distribution is known as continual learning problems.
- The meta directional update is conceptually similar to the formulation in Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Reptile. There is no head-to-head discussion with these two methods and direct comparison in terms of formulation. Especially, This work has no empirical comparison with these methods (that can be applied directly to the problem at hand).
- It is not straightforward to undertand the empirical results in Figure 3 with a little description on the experimental setup. The competitive advantage of FOML is to learn without task boundaries, but the problem still has task boundaries and the same partition as in the previous work  by Finn et al. (2019) to compare between online algorithms. In my opinion, even though the task information is not explicitly given for learning purposes but FOML is exposed with task information indirectly due to the setup described in Section 6, especially with the task partitions.
- There is a big question: why does TOE consistently perform poorly on average among all other methods? Why is this method performing really bad given the fact that it can access all past tasks? As mentioned in the paper, this approach trains the model using all tasks in the large buffer. 
- There is minimum information about LwF, iCARL, and MOCA on how they are implemented for the online meta-learning setup. Please elaborate on how to adapt these methods for the online meta-learning setting. The supplementary material also does not contain this information.
- Also, the use of a Siamese Network needs to be explained for reproducibility. Moreover, there are no citations for this type of network as well.
- There is an inconsistency in writing the proposed method. In formulation, there is a number $K$ for regularization but it is omitted in Algorithm 1.
- The paper needs some corrections:
-- Please fix the manuscript with numbered equations. The number stops at 5.
-- Typo and grammatical errors: varaint, a online data stream, evaulate.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There some unclear messages in problem description, experiments, and comparison to SOTA. The novelty also needs to be justified by providing discussion and comparison with EWC and Reptile. There are some missing information needed to replicate the results from other methods and the proposed method.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has some potentials to address online meta-learning problems with no task boundaries. However, there are some unclear messages and problem descriptions in text. Also, there are some inconsistencies between the claims and the experiments to prove them.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to R3
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed feedback! We added more explanations to make the paper more clear and fixed the errors in the equations and typos. We discuss this and the other questions raised in your review below. Please let us know if this response addresses your concerns, or if there is anything else that we can add or modify.

R3.1 Clarity: 

Task boundary definition : Thanks for raising these questions. We addressed your concerns in the revised paper. Mainly, in this work we define a task as a set of samples which share some similar discrete variables. For example, a task can be created by a group of class labels, or semantic categories or even a time stamp. In our experiments and other baseline methods, tasks have boundaries. However, our algorithm (FOML) does not need to know these boundary labels, while previous works need to access this information from their meta-learning updates (FTL, FTML). Especially, In Finn et al. (FTML) Algorithm 2, line 4, their method needs to sample tasks from the buffer to compute the meta-gradients. This requires explicit knowledge of which part of the buffer belongs to which task.

Gradual changes in tasks : The main goal of this work is to bridge the gap between meta learning and online learning. Therefore, our formulation might not fall under the classical definition of meta learning or online learning. In addition to that, in the paper we explicitly stated that we focus on online learning rather than continual learning. While both learning problems tackle the online stream of data, continual learning focuses on catastrophic forgetting, while online learning focuses more on the fast adaptation problem. In this work, we use meta learning to fastly adapt to new tasks in a fully online manner. However, we have also included comparisons with continual learning methods. In Fig 3, we have compared our method with LwF and iCaRL and the experiments showed that our method performs better than these continual learning methods on this setting.  

Interpreting Fig 3 : As mentioned previously (a), tasks have boundaries. The difference is where the method needs to access this boundary label or not. We will clarify this confusion in the paper. In all our experiments, all the baselines and our method were trained with a sequence of tasks with boundaries. Only FOML (our method) does not use this boundary information when training. We believe there is no implicit information about the task boundary leaked into the algorithm in the experimental setup in Section 6. We would appreciate it if the reviewer can give more details about this concern.  

The big question : It is very common in deep networks, that an expert model trained on a specific task would perform better than a general model trained on all the tasks (Jurjo et al. Learning to see by looking at noise). Therefore, since TOE is trained on lots of tasks, it might have poor performance compared to a model finetined on the task, which is being evaluated. However, we agree with the reviewer that with lots of training and larger models, TOE would converge to the same performance as any other online training methods. While this is true, in this work we keep the same computational complexity for all methods and only study the adaptation speed. In this setting, TOE is slower compared to other baselines. 

There is minimum information about LwF, iCARL : At the time of submission we have already submitted a supplementary materials document with additional details about baselines, network architecture and ablation experiments. If the reviewer requires more information, could you please share what information is missing, we will include it in the revision.  https://openreview.net/attachment?id=eLxADkHrBcR&name=supplementary_material 

First order approximation : We have included a comparison with FOML and a first order approximation of FOML (equivalent to FOML+Reptile) in the appendix. In FOML+R, we simply compute the meta gradient as the direction towards the last inner-loop parameters. Our experiments shows that, while the FOML+R can learn new tasks, it is still slower than the FOML method. We will evaluate FOML+R on various datasets and report it in the final version of the paper. 

Numbered equations and typos: Thanks for pointing out the mistakes in the text and equations. We have fixed the equation numbers and typos in the revised manuscript.

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
We want to thank the authors for providing the response. 

Some concerns still remain after reading the rebuttal and revision:

(1). Considering a comment by R-K4eM, there is a similar concern about classic online learning and comparison in the revision. The revision and rebuttal still failed to differentiate this work with previous work and discuss its significance. This is crucial to understand the setting and how to make it disctinct from classic online learning. As task boundaries are not significantly important in the setting, some readers might misunderstood that the FTL method is implemented as standard online learning but with an additional memory buffer. I would recommend that the online learning paragraph in Section 3 includes the original version of FTL.

(2). Related to (1), this raises another confusion to "meta-learning without task boundaries" which sounds like standard/classical online learning. The response below stated that the task boundaries might be labels and FOML does not need to know boundary labels. Actually, this statement is vague as the loss function $\mathcal{L}(\phi^{j-1}, D_{tr}^{j} )$ needs $D_{tr}$ containing inputs and labels. In my opinion, this might implicitly provide task boundaries. 

(3). Related to the performance of TOE, I have to disagree that learning on all task might degrade the performance for a specific task. As understood in continual learning literature, one task might be relevant to another task resulting knowledge accumulation and better generalization (see Hadsell et al.). Based on observation of continual learning literature (with gradual changes over time), this can occur only when a deep learning model deals with a very limited number of classes. 

(4). The revision still does not contain any implementation information of continual learning methods (e.g.,  LwF, iCARL, and MOCA) for FOML. As these methods are not originally targeted for FOML, it would be better to include implementation for reproducibility. The question above clearly stated that the implementation details are missing, and they are not provided in supplementary materials.

(5). After revision, there are some grammatical errors and typos:
- our method continuously update meta-parameters
- a meta-weights
- a model will all

Hadsell et al., "Embracing Change: Continual Learning in Deep Neural Networks".

content.title: Response to R3
content.comment:
1) We agree that classic online learning can be defined without tasks [3]. The particular online meta-learning setting that we study, where task boundaries are not known, can be viewed as a structural assumption on top of the fully general online learning setting. The structural assumption is that the underlying problems consist of tasks, which change over time in a way that is not provided to the learner. This makes it possible to use meta-learning to improve significantly over fully general online learning methods. We will clarify this distinction in the next revision of the paper. To summarize the distinction in our problem setting: Compared to prior work on online learning, our method tackles a meta-learning setting where the observed stream of data is produced by (gradually) changing underlying tasks. Compared to prior work on online *meta-learning*, which assume known task boundaries, our method does not assume that the task boundaries are known. Thus our assumptions are stronger than classic online learning, but weaker than prior online meta-learning methods. We strongly believe that learning without task boundaries is significantly important for online meta-learning learning in particular. As we have discussed in the paper, many if not all tasks in the real world do not come with task boundaries and there have been a lot of works in this direction focusing on online learning without tasks [3,4,5,6]. 

2) Tasks in our experiments can vary in terms of what changes. For Rainbow-MNIST, the labels don't change across tasks, just the color of the digits. For the CIFAR100 tasks, the label is class-agnostic, only indicating whether two images have the same class or not. Different tasks require making this same vs. not same classification for different types of objects. Our algorithm, which does not get any labels of such boundaries, is unaware of when this change occurs. By contrast, prior methods like FTML explicitly receive task boundaries, where they reset the inner loop weights back to the meta-weights and restart adaptation. While it's certainly possible for a model to figure out task boundaries from examining the images and labels, we believe that the problem formulation does not by itself provide any leakage of privileged information -- that is, the labels don't indicate when the task has changed by themselves at least in these tasks. However, if we misunderstood your question, please let us know where you believe such leakage might occur.

3) It's definitely true that TOE can enjoy benefits from forward transfer, and indeed as shown in Fig 3, with longer training times, it might in the end have the same error rate as FOML. However, FOML gets to that point much faster than TOE, because it can take advantage of learned fast adaptation. That is, while TOE needs to train until it generalizes to each new observation, FOML can adapt to a recent context to get to lower error rates significantly faster. This observation is aligned with the idea of experts and generalized models, a model fine tuned on a specific task (experts) would perform better than a generalized model [2]. Even in the continual learning literature, we have seen that while some tasks help others (forward transfer), it can hurt also (e.g. negative backward transfer) [1]. Adaptation provides for specialization within each task. So while we agree that in principle TOE can do well (as indeed it does asymptotically), we believe that this does not contradict our findings, though we will definitely clarify the corresponding claims in the paper.

4) Here, we provide a very brief summary for each continual learning method (we will include more extensive descriptions in the revised paper):

    LwF : First we train a model $\theta$ on FOML objective (e.g. for Online-CIFAR100, we use binary cross entropy loss) for the task t. Then for task t+1, we freeze the weights of this model and initialize $\phi$ with the same parameters as $\theta$. During the training of task t+1, the model is optimized over two loss functions: a) the FOML objective, b) A KL-divergence loss between the predictions from the frozen $\theta$ model and the current $\phi$ model. This allows the new model to remember the features/predictions about old tasks.

    iCaRL : iCaRL follows a similar idea along the lines of LwF, and adds an additional memory buffer to store a subset of the past data. We use the same implementation as LwF and a 3rd objective, which samples some past data from the memory and computes a loss on the new model parameters ($\phi$).

    MOCA : We used the official implementation of MOCA with “class” as problem setting within the PCOC (probabilistic clustering for online classification) setting. Each sample is passed through an encoding network and Bayesian density estimation is applied on each class in this feature space. We only set the switch time at the first task and keep it off throughout the learning. 

5) We will fix the grammatical errors and typos.

content.title: Response to R2
content.comment: The focus of our work is not on proving bounds on regret, our aim is to propose a practical algorithm for meta-learning in the online setting, with an empirical evaluation. We believe that this is well in line with the standard for applied machine learning research. The definition of regret is provided to specify a criterion by which online meta-learning methods have been evaluated in prior work. We can certainly remove this definition if this is the main issue, as it is not central to the paper's contribution, which is a practical algorithm for online meta-learning and a comparative evaluation with previously proposed methods, which shows that our algorithm attains better results across a range of image-based tasks. We believe that algorithms that outperform prior works and are evaluated empirically are of interest to the ICLR community.

content.title: Post rebuttal
content.comment: I thank the authors for their feedback. I understand the claim made by the authors, but then I would at least: 1) indeed remove all mathematical concepts uselessly introduced, and 2) make clear that not assuming the task boundaries to be known also prevents from deriving any theoretical results. The interest of the proposed framework then becomes more questionable, and solving the tradeoff "keeping task boundaries VS abandoning any guarantee" is far from being obvious to me. I am open to discussion on this point though, and wait for the interaction with other reviewers to update my score.

content.title: Response to R2
content.comment:
Thank you for the reply. We can certainly clarify in the paper that our work does not aim to or attempt to present any theoretical results (we cannot edit the paper at this stage in the process, but can revise the final). We would prefer not to write that the lack of task boundaries itself **prevents** deriving theoretical results, because we don't know if that is true or not -- we make no attempt in this paper to derive theoretical results and have no idea if that is feasible or not, and therefore would prefer not to speculate on how difficult or easy that would be.

In regard to unnecessary mathematical concepts, we can certainly remove anything that is not useful for the exposition in the paper. Is this in reference specifically to the definition of regret? If so, we can certainly remove that definition.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a method to continually adapt a deep network to smoothly-changing tasks, by meta-learning a regularizer online. This regularizer consists of a L2 loss that binds the online-adapted parameters and (meta-learned) reference parameters together.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The motivation for the method is clear and makes sense, given the problem setting of online (continual) learning. The method seems novel, and has good experimental results in the analyzed settings.

Weaknesses:
- The main weakness is a series of mistakes in the equations, which makes them hard to parse, and the textual description of the method not being very clear.
- The appendix seems to be missing (!) so important implementation details are missing; this harms the reproducibility.
- Some discussion of related work is missing, but this is a smaller issue.
- Comparison with the most related Continual Learning methods would be better, namely those that also train online with a buffer of past samples: Tiny Episodic Memories, and GDumb.

The paper would benefit from discussing the relation between the proposed method, of a fast-learning network trailed by a (meta-learned) slow-learning "anchor" network, and others with a similar set-up. One such example is:
- Zhang et al., "Lookahead Optimizer: k steps forward, 1 step back", NeurIPS 2019
Other works that focus on learning by "self-distillation" (where usually the two models are described as teacher and student) should also be discussed:
- Caron et al., "Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers", 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are several aspects of the paper that are unclear or have mistakes, described below. The method seems novel and the paper would be high quality if it were not for the unclear aspects/mistakes. There are important implementation details omitted, as it seems that the appendix was cut off.

I will now list the unclear parts, mostly equation mistakes:

- In the FTML equation (after eq. 5), phi is used in both argmins. This is nonsensical, because it means that the first argmin does not contain its minimizee variable at all; and if it was meant to be implicitly present via the second line, its reuse in the second line's argmin prevents this. This makes the whole equation impossible to parse.

- In the same equation, the LHS of the second line uses time index t-1, but the RHS does not -- so what changes between iterations? I can guess that Tau might need to be indexed using t, but this is unclear.

- In the first equation of section 5.2 (the authors really ought to number their equations), the first term in brackets does not contain theta; so the gradient of this term w.r.t. theta will be zero (wiping out this term). If there is a dependence, how is it achieved? This needs to be made explicit in the equation.

- Algorithm 1, lines 6-7: Missing j index in D (minor).

- Algorithm 1, lines 9-10: The notation \phi_\theta is used for the first time without explanation. Furthermore, it is used inconsistently -- in line 10, the theta is missing. If this was not used in all the equations so far, what role does it play here? This needs to be harmonized or explained in the text.

- Page 3: In the discussion of Continual Learning (via meta-learning), contrasting "batch-mode meta-learning" with the proposal should be made more clear, since at this point one does not have enough context to understand what is meant by "batch-mode" in this case.

- Page 5: "Note that this is subtly different from FTL in the classic online learning setting, due to the difference in problem formulation." - This is not enough; what is this classic setting and how is this different?

- Page 5: "Although FTML can enable fast adaptation, the model needs to be “reset” at each task, essentially creating a “branch” on each task and maintaining two independent learning processes: an
adaptation process, whose result is discarded completely at the end of the task, and a meta-training process, which does not influence the current task at all, and is only used for forward transfer into future tasks." This whole phrase is very hard to parse. It also does not follow the next conclusion that the method is "not fully online".
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper seems to present a nice method but requires some work to make the explanations more clear and correct notation mistakes. The missing appendix gives the impression that the submission was a bit rushed. It could also be made more complete in terms of related work. As it is, this paper is very borderline, but can be published if the authors can visibly correct all the mentioned mistakes, and improve it generally.

content.title: Response to R1
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed feedback! We have revised the paper to fix the errors in the equations and added detailed explanations to the equations. The supplementary material is already attached with the paper, with a different link. We discuss this and the other questions raised in your review below. Please let us know if this response addresses your concerns, or if there is anything else that we can add or modify.

R1.1 Equations and Clearity : 

FTML equation (Eq 6,7) : Thanks for pointing out this mistake, we have fixed the argmin statement in Eq 6. The way FTML (the prior method) operates is that it first trains a model (\phi_{MAML}^{t-1})  with a MAML-style algorithm with the data from t-1 tasks. Then take these pretrained weights (\phi_{MAML}^{t-1}) and finetunes on the new data from task t. Therefore Eq 6. optimizes the pretrained MAML parameters (\phi_{MAML}^{t-1}). In addition to that, we also added the LHS of Eq 7 with time index t-1. As the reviewer suggested, the \tau data distribution is from the sequences of data up to t-1 tasks. Therefore, the MAML model is trained on the data from t-1 tasks. 
Eq 10 : During the meta updates, we compute the loss using the online parameters \phi^j and a regularization loss. The dependance of \phi^j on \theta comes from the previous online update in Eq 9. Since our algorithm continually updates online and meta parameters, the online updates use regularization with \theta and vice versa. Therefore the dependance on the online parameters comes from the regularization terms. 

Algorithm 1 : We included \phi_\theta to show the dependance of \phi on \theta. However, since we have discussed this dependance on Eq 10 as the reviewer pointed out, we will remove this notation and keep it very simple. 

Batch-mode meta-training : We have revised the paper to give more clear explanations about batch-mode meta-training. Most of the previous works (Nagabandi et al, Javed & White, Harrison et al. ) train a single model at every task boundary using the past data (batch-mode, by batching all the seen data). Afterwards, these methods finetune the pretrained weights to adapt to the new task. This batch-mode training requires knowledge of the task boundary and the meta-learning is done discreetly at every task boundary. However, our method trains a single meta model over time and continually updates its parameters with meta-updates at every time step. 

FTML fast adaptation : As shown in Fig 1, the standard online meta learning method (e.g. FTML) follows the recipe of meta-learning at the task boundary and adapts to a new task and then completely discards these adopted parameters. This creates branches at every task boundary and the parameter trajectory is not continuous (since these methods reset back to meta parameters after the adaptation). On the other hand, our method (as shown on the right side of Fig 1) continually updates meta-parameters without switching to adaptation and resetting process. We have updated the manuscript with additional explanations. 

Additional discussion : We have included an additional section to discuss the similarities and differences between our work and Zhang et al. and Caron et al. Apart from the fact that these works aim to solve different tasks, the main difference between these works and ours is that our meta update is based on the gradient of the gradients.  Zhang et al. use k inner-loop updates to find an optimal direction for the outer-loop parameters, and Caron et al. use exponential moving average to update the slow-weights. In both cases, the slow-weights are updated based on the first order approximation of the meta update. Compared to these works, our method actually computes the 2nd order derivatives of the online trajectory and updates the meta-parameters. Of course, computing the 2nd order derivative is computationally complex, and in that sense the first order approximations proposed by Zhang et al. and Caron et al. may be preferable in cases where such gradients are computationally difficult to obtain.

R1.2 Supplementary material: We have already included supplementary material at the time of our submission with the details about the network architectures, baseline methods and additional experiments. 
 (https://openreview.net/attachment?id=eLxADkHrBcR&name=supplementary_material)

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
I'd like to thank the authors for answering my questions. I'll focus on the ones that are still not addressed either by the comment or the revised paper:

1. The main equations of the paper, now Eq. 6-7, still contain what seems like a nonsensical recursivity that is hard to reconcile. Namely, $\phi^{t-1}_{MAML}$ is both defined as the argument of the minimization of Eq. 6 (so it's a free variable) and as the result of another minimization in Eq. 7 (so it's constrained to a single value). Since this is the main contribution of the paper it really needs to be as rigorous as possible.

2. Dependence of $\phi$ in $\theta$: Algorithm 1 still uses inconsistently $\phi_\theta$ which was not defined (line 12). I'd suggest that the authors use the standard notation for functional dependence, which is just $\phi(\theta)$.

3. The claim made about the difference from "classic online learning" in page 5 needs appropriate citations and clarification, to know exactly what work is being compared with, a point that I made earlier.

4. Although the authors have done well to include a few baselines from Continual Learning, and explained the difference from MOCA, there are several more works in CL that also aim to do away with task boundaries. I would like to ask the authors to cite and discuss these works, which are the closest to the proposed method, and also provide a brief summary of the differences in a comment.
- Aljundi et al., "Task-Free Continual Learning", CVPR 2019
- Aljundi et al., "Gradient based sample selection for online continual learning", NeurIPS 2019
- Koh et al., "Online Continual Learning on Class Incremental Blurry Task Configuration with Anytime Inference", ICLR 2022

As an additional note, the revised text that was added is very unpolished, filled with language and formatting errors -- I expect the authors to do proper proofreading if the paper is accepted.

content.title: Response to R1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for giving valuable feedback.
- We will revise Eq 6 & 7. However, we want to make it clear that Eq 6, 7 is not our method, these equations present background on how a prior method (FTML, Finn et al.) addresses online meta-learning. FTML first solves Eq 6, obtains a set of parameters for $\phi_{MAML}^{t-1}$, and then initializes Eq  7 from these parameters. We will replace the $\phi_{MAML}^{t-1}$ in Eq 6 with an optimization parameter $\phi$ and say that $\phi$ will be initialized with $\phi_{MAML}^{t-1}$ from Eq 6 at the start of the optimization process in Eq 7. We hope this explains the prior FTML method. We will make these changes in the final version of the paper, since we are not allowed to make any changes now.

- Thanks for the suggestion, we will update Algorithm 1 with standard notations and replace the $\phi_{\theta}$ with $\phi(\theta)$.

- We will cite appropriate papers to clarify the comparison with classic online learning. We will cite and discuss these following works [4,5,6], but please let us know if any other citations would be helpful.

- We will address these papers in detail in our final version of the paper. Here we provide a brief summary of similarities and differences between these works and ours.

The learning setting in Aljundi et al. [1] is similar to our method. However, there are two main notable differences. a) While Aljundi et al. [1] does not require any knowledge about the task boundaries, their method implicitly finds these boundaries by looking at the loss curve, and once it identifies a boundary it updates the weights as previous task-aware methods. On the other hand, our method does not require any knowledge about the task boundary and our method does not actually attempt to find these boundaries at all. b) While their way of updating importance weight and our meta updates conceptually focus on the same goal, our method learns these weights in an end-to-end fashion rather than using exponential moving average as in [1]. In addition to that, their buffer is mined based on hard samples and ours is simply built on recent observations.

Aljundi et al. [2] proposed a gradient based method to select samples in the online stream in GEM (Gradient Episodic Memory). Their proposed sample selection strategy allow them to apply GEM constraint on fewer samples. Their greedy version assigns scores to each sample in the buffer based on the current batch and updates them as a Bernoulli event. Our method on the other hand uses a simple random sampling strategy. Of course, our method can incorporate any sampling strategy in principle. We will compare various sampling techniques and do an ablation on the paper. 

Koh et al. [3] proposes a new online continual learning setup, where in a class incremental fashion some classes are added over time while some classes exist in the online stream all the time. Please note that both [2,3] optimize for continual learning, hence these methods try to minimize catastrophic forgetting. Especially in [3], the online stream is directly stored/discarded into a buffer. Afterwards, they sample from this buffer and update their model, such that it remembers past tasks and current tasks. Compared to these works our method focuses on doing better at the current task only and uses the past data to acquire new knowledge faster. In continual learning literature terms, these methods optimize from forward and backward transfer of knowledge. While if the goal is to perform better at the task at hand, it is essential to do well on forward transfer. This what our method does, it uses past knowledge **not** for doing better at past tasks (which is not useful for online learning), but for doing better at new tasks. 

    [1] Aljundi et al., "Task-Free Continual Learning", CVPR 2019
    [2] Aljundi et al., "Gradient based sample selection for online continual learning", NeurIPS 2019
    [3] Koh et al., "Online Continual Learning on Class Incremental Blurry Task Configuration with Anytime Inference", ICLR 2022
    [4] Hannan et al., Approximation to Bayes risk in repeated play, 1957
    [5] Cesa-Bianchi et al., Prediction, learning, and games , 2006
    [6] Finn et al., Online meta-learning, 2019.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper tackles a novel problem of fully online meta-learning. The main difference of the proposed problem setting from the previous online meta-learning problem is that it does not assume clear boundaries between the tasks and the task distribution can gradually change over time. To tackle this new problem, the authors propose a meta-learning framework similar to Reptile with a data buffer, which regularizes the task-specific parameters to be close to the meta-parameters. The experimental validation of the method on multiple benchmarks verifies the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The paper received split reviews, with three of the reviewers recommending, or leaning toward rejection and one recommending an acceptance. The reviewers considered the tackled problem as interesting as well as challenging and relevant to many real-world problems, the proposed online meta-learning framework with no task boundary as somewhat novel, and the experimental validation as convincing.

However, the reviewers had the following critical concerns
- Although the paper proposes a novel problem setting, its definition is rather unclear - the role of the task boundaries and the gradual change of the tasks, are not well defined with formal descriptions.
- The proposed regularization-based meta-learning framework is similar to Reptile, but there is no discussion or comparison against it. 
- The experimental section does not provide much insight into how the proposed method works, as it is lacking in-depth analysis.
- There is minimal information of how the baselines are modified for the fully online meta-learning setting. 
- Despite the similarity of the proposed problem to task-free continual learning, there is no comparison against state-of-the-art continual learning methods.

The authors’ responses dealt with some of the issues, but did not provide clear answers to some of the questions (missing comparison with Reptile and task-free continual learning methods). Therefore, the reviewers remained unconvinced even after the rebuttal and kept their original ratings on the paper.  

I also find the paper not yet fully ready for publication - 1) it is unclear how the proposed problem differs from task-free continual learning (is it assuming a stationary task distribution as Reviewer a6XH mentioned?), 2) how the proposed method differs from Reptile besides the lack of task boundaries, 3) the paper provides little insights as to how the proposed method works. However the authors did not provide clear answers to these questions. Some of the arguments from the authors are also inaccurate, such as the statement that continual learning mostly focuses on catastrophic forgetting with little emphasis on rapid adaptation, or forward transfer. However, these have been important goals for continual learning since its inception.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score:
- The paper lacks clear descriptions of the problem setting, and how it differs from task-free continual learning. 
- There is little discussion of, and experimental comparison against relevant works on task-free continual learning and Reptile, which has a very similar objective.
